Viewport · three.js, vendored · still SVG underneath

A viewport is mostly its controls

Four plates standing on a lit ground, and seven docked control groups around them. The subject is the least interesting part: what this page is for is where a control is allowed to sit, what it is allowed to act on, and how a reader tells apart the three different things that all mean “bigger”. With scripting off the same subject is shown as a flat isometric still and the page reads correctly.

1What is on the stagelive nowA tile, drawn as four plates on a ground plane, so that every verb the controls use — closer, apart, above — has something to be relative to.

The subject is one tile: nine squares, built up in four passes. Each pass adds to what the pass below it left, so the finished thing is a single flat image and the only way to see what any one pass contributed is to lift it off the others. That is what apart is for, and it is the entire reason this subject was chosen over an abstract shape.

The earlier version of this page floated four shapes on a dark rectangle. It read as a picture of an object rather than as a view onto a scene, and the reason is worth stating plainly: every viewport control is relative, and with nothing underneath the subject, none of the verbs had an object. Closer to what. Apart from what. So there is a ground now, and it is drawn — a rule grid, in the same tokens as everything else on the site — and the plates stand on it.

1—
Fig. 1 · four plates, one tile · 4 up · apart 0 · rung 2
In handFormp4Choose the tint for the Form plate. One swatch is one identity colour, and the plate keeps it through every other control.

Every control above is docked inside the frame. A rail underneath a picture is a toolbar belonging to the page; a rail inside the frame is a control belonging to the view. Put four of these side by side and the difference stops being a preference: external toolbars stack into a wall of buttons that no longer says which frame each one drives.

2Seven places, and what each one ownsposition is meaningA control's dock says what it acts on. Reader finds reset bottom-right on the map, finds it bottom-right on the model.

The split is by what the control acts on, never by what it looks like. Two controls that both use a plus glyph belong in different docks if one moves the eye and the other moves the subject, and the dock is what tells them apart before the reader has hovered anything.

position is the label

Table 6The seven docks of a viewport framethe contract · every frame on the site
DockOwnsTypically
Top leftIdentity. What this frame is, and which of the two kinds it is.Name, mode, the subject's address.
Top rightWhat the frame does to the subject's presentation.Fill, tone, projection, units.
Left railWhere the eye stands. Never the subject.Closer, further, home.
Right railWhich of the subject's layers are standing.One control per layer, named.
Bottom leftWhat the frame is doing, as distinct from what it is looking at.Turn, edges, editing, follow, play.
Bottom centreNavigation of the subject's own geometry.Apart, together, step, seek.
Bottom rightThe readout, and anything that acts on the frame itself.Frame time, scale, fullscreen, reset.

Fig. 2 The two side rails are the pair a flat viewport does not need. A map has no layers standing above each other and a chart has no eye to move, so on those frames the rails are simply absent — the docks are a vocabulary, not a template every frame has to fill.

3Three kinds of bigger1 glyph, 1 axisThe eye moves, the subject spreads, or the frame rescales. They are three axes and they must never share a mark.

This is the one thing a viewport gets wrong most often, and it is invisible until someone uses the thing. Closer moves the eye and changes nothing about the subject. Apart changes the subject's own geometry and leaves the eye where it was. Fill changes how much of the frame the subject occupies and moves neither. All three make the picture bigger. All three are different questions.

Table 7The three axes, their marks, and their docksthree axes · three marks · three docks
AxisMarkDockMoves
CameramagnifierLeft railthe eye
Spreadplus and minusBottom centrethe subject
FillexpandTop rightneither — the frame rescales

Turning is the mouse's job, not a button's

Distance is on a rail because it is a value with a range and a reader wants it to stop where they put it. Orientation is not that. A reader turning a model is aiming, and aiming through two buttons is aiming with the lights off — so the frame is dragged directly: press anywhere on the stage and the subject follows the pointer, wheel over it and the eye steps in and out on the same rail the magnifier drives. Pointer events rather than mouse events, so a finger and a mouse are one code path, and the pointer is captured, so a drag that leaves the canvas keeps turning instead of sticking the subject half way round.

Two limits, and both are about not being able to get back. The pitch is clamped short of either pole, because a camera that goes over the top puts the ground plane above the subject and every reader reads that as the picture having broken. And Home restores the orientation as well as the distance — that is the whole licence for a free camera. A view a reader can lose themselves in needs one press that undoes it; without that press, dragging is a trap and the two buttons really were the safer answer.

viewer.ts
const r = Math.cos(el) * d;
cam.position.set(Math.sin(az) * r, Math.sin(el) * d + 0.35, Math.cos(az) * r);
cam.lookAt(0, 1.0, 0);
el = Math.max(0.08, Math.min(1.45, el));   // never over the pole
The magnifier is reserved for the camera. It is the one mark on the page that a reader arrives already knowing, and spending it on anything other than distance costs more than any other glyph decision on a viewport. Plus and minus are the general pair and can mean whatever their dock says they mean; the magnifier cannot.

4A rail reports, and a rail refuses5 stops, shownA discrete control prints its own position and disables itself at its ends, before it is pressed rather than after.

Both rails on the stage are discrete: five camera rungs, five spread stops. Two things follow from that and neither is optional. The rail prints where it is — 2/4 under the buttons — because a control with five positions and no readout is a control the reader has to press to the end to find out where they were. And the rail disables itself at its ends, so it says where its limits are before it is pressed. A button that silently does nothing is the version of this that makes a reader think the page is broken.

The disabled button stays in the rail rather than being removed. A rail that changes length as it is used moves the next control under a pointer that was already on its way, and gets pressed twice by accident.

viewer.ts
const dis = (act, off) => document.querySelectorAll('[data-act="' + act + '"]')
  .forEach(b => { b.disabled = off; });
dis("sp-", stop === 0);            // says so before it is pressed
dis("sp+", stop === STOPS - 1);
The last layer cannot be put away

Turning off every plate leaves an empty stage, which is a state with no way out that looks exactly like a crash. The layer rail refuses the last one standing. Refusing is better than confirming: a dialog to ask whether the reader meant to empty the frame is a dialog about a thing nobody wants.

A tool is a glyph, and the cluster is one object

None of these marks carries a fill. A filled badge is how the rest of this site says here is a value, and it has a state; a tool is not a value, and thirty filled lozenges scattered over a picture read as data laid on the subject rather than as controls belonging to the frame. So the fill and the border go, the glyph stays, and the states are told in the mark itself: ink-muted at rest, accent under the pointer, and an amber fill when it is on. Two colours and two jobs: teal arrives with the pointer and leaves with it, so it can never be read as a setting; amber says this is the one being talked about, which is the same thing it says everywhere else on the site. Black fill was the old answer to on and it is not one — it turns the glyph into a hole and puts a third colour on a frame that has two.

The one exception is the layer rail, and it is the exception that proves the rule — there the colour is the plate's identity, so the fill goes and the tint stays, on the glyph. That is the same trade tile makes: a neutral frame, and the selected mark carrying the colour.

Tools that act on one axis are then drawn as one object: a single outline round the cluster with hairlines between the marks, not five separately bordered pills. Five outlines say five axes and leave the reader counting to find out otherwise; one outline says this is the camera and the divisions inside it say and it has three hands. It is also what makes the help numbers cheap — there are five things on the frame to number, because there are five objects.

tokens-extra.ts
.vp .badge.bare{background:none;border-color:transparent;box-shadow:none}
.vp [data-act] .badge{color:var(--ink-muted)}
.vp .vp-pick > .mk:hover .badge{color:var(--accent)}
.vp .vt[aria-pressed="true"] .badge,
.vp .vp-pick > input:checked ~ .mk .badge{color:var(--ink);
  background:var(--pastel-amber);border-color:var(--stroke-amber)}
.vp-btns{gap:0;border:1px solid var(--rule-soft);border-radius:4px}
.vp-btns > * + *{border-left:1px solid var(--rule-soft)}

A tool with more than two answers opens a drawn one

A glyph that cycles is only honest where the answers are two. Past that the reader is pressing to find out, which is the interaction equivalent of reading a list by deleting it one line at a time — twelve tints reached by twelve presses is eleven wrong pictures on the way to the right one. So the four marks beside the circle-i are not cycles. Each opens a small panel, and each panel is drawn: the tint tool is swatches, the shape tool is shapes, the layer tool is the stack in the order the stack is in, and the mode tool draws both sides of the choice so the reader can see the other one before standing in it.

The rule underneath is the one the panel section states and it applies to a rail just as hard: the control wears the value's own face. Nobody converts p7 back into a colour, and six shape names are six things to picture and then match. A word is the right control only where the value genuinely has no other face.

Table 8bThe four tools beside the circle-i, and what each drawsfour tools · one cluster · top right
ToolDrawsAnswers
Palettetwelve swatches, then the four plates the choice derivesone identity, and the ramp it implies
Layersone row per plate, in stack orderfour transparencies, per plate
Shapesix outlines, then three frames at three sizesthe subject's form, and how much frame it takes
Modeboth states, side by side, drawnviewing or editing
A picker that changes four things shows the four

Choosing one swatch sets a whole ramp, and a grid of twelve with no preview reads as twelve wrong answers to a question about one colour. The palette panel therefore ends in the four plates it just derived. Any control whose one input has more than one output owes the reader that row.

5Help is a mode, not a hoverthe circle-i, top rightA tooltip answers a question about a control the reader has already found. It does not answer the one they ask first.

Every mark in these rails used to carry a hover plate with two lines: what the control is called, and what pressing it does. It was well meant and it was in the way. The plate opens beside the rail, which is the space the pointer travels through to reach the control next to the one being read, so a reader working down a column of five tools crossed a note on each move and pushed it aside four times. A note that has to be dodged to reach the tool has made the tool worse.

It also answered the wrong question. A tooltip is an answer about one control, and it can only be asked by someone already pointing at that control. The question a reader asks first is asked standing back from the frame: what am I looking at, and where is the thing I want. No amount of per-control hover text answers it, because reading fourteen notes one at a time is not the same act as seeing the shape of the thing.

So the notes came off the controls and became a mode. The in the top right raises a number on every cluster and one legend saying what each cluster owns and what is in it — five circles, in the places the clusters really stand. Out of help mode there is nothing at all between the pointer and the glyph, which is the state the frame is in for the whole of the time any work is being done in it.

Number the cluster, not the tool

Fourteen circles over five plates is a second interface laid across the first one, and the reader has to find the number before they can look it up. Five is a map. It is also the honest unit: a dock owns an axis, and what someone standing back has to learn is which axis lives where — not which of two adjacent buttons is the plus.

Three rules hold the mode together. The numbers are furniture: while they are up the tools are inert, so a reader counting clusters against the legend cannot switch one by pointing at it. Closing the help leaves the frame in exactly the state it was opened in — help that edits the reader's work is worse than no help. And it is a checkbox and two labels, not script, so it survives scripting being off: the still is precisely where a reader knows least about what they are looking at, and the least defensible place to lose the help.

viewer.ts
<input type="checkbox" class="vp-helpck" id="vw-helpck">
...
<label class="vp-helpmk" for="vw-helpck"
       aria-label="Help mode -- number every cluster and say what it owns">…</label>
...
<span class="vp-grp"><span class="hn" aria-hidden="true">2</span>
  <div class="vp-btns col">…</div>
</span>
tokens-extra.ts
.hn{display:none;position:absolute;left:-7px;top:-7px;z-index:19;
  background:var(--tip-paper);border:1px solid var(--ink-muted)}
.h1:checked ~ .vp-lm .hn,.h2:checked ~ .vp-lm .hn{display:flex}
.h1:checked ~ .vp-lm .vp-grp{box-shadow:0 0 0 3px var(--rule)}

Two presses, because there are two questions

The circle-i is a cycle of three, not a switch. Press it once and every cluster grows an outlined number over the live frame — nothing is covered, nothing is dimmed, and every control still works. That is the state for the reader whose question is which of these is the fourth one: they are reading the numbers in order to use the tools, not instead of using them.

Press it again and the map comes up over the frame. That is a different question — what is this thing, and where does each part live — and it is the one a list alone cannot answer. A legend can say “Camera, left rail”; it cannot tell a reader who has not yet looked away from the middle of the picture which of the two columns the left rail is. The wireframe answers that in a glance, and the numbered rows underneath then say what each cluster owns. A third press puts it away.

Outlined, never filled

A solid disc on this site is a badge, and a badge is a value that belongs to the thing it sits on. Fill the help numbers and they read as data about the subject rather than as a caption about the frame — so they are hollow, and while they are up each cluster carries the faintest wash to be findable against a moving picture, coming up to a readable outline only under the pointer.

Three radios and three labels, each pointing at the next state, with only the current state's label rendered. It costs one input more than a checkbox and it buys a cycle that runs with scripting off — which is the case that matters, because a still frame with no captions is exactly where a reader knows least.

While the numbers are up, pointing at a cluster opens a small note beside it — the number, the cluster's name, the one line of what it owns, and the keys it contains. It opens away from its own rail, so it never leaves the frame and never covers the thing it is describing, and it is inert: no pointer events, no press, nothing to dismiss. It exists only in the first help state. In normal use the same hover does what hover should do on a tool, which is nothing but a cursor change.

Amber is the subject, teal is the pointer

Two colours, two jobs, everywhere on the frame. Amber means this is the thing being explained — the lit circle-i, the numbers, the wash under a numbered cluster, the ring the tour is standing on. Teal means this is the thing under your hand — hover, and only hover. Because they never overlap, a reader can tell at a glance whether a highlight is something the page is saying or something they are doing, without being told.

A tour is a caption that moves

The map answers where is everything in one picture, but it cannot pace a reader through five clusters in order. So the card ends with one door — Walk me through it — and pressing it drops back to the first state, not the map. That is deliberate: a tour that keeps the map up would put a card over the very controls it is pointing at. The frame comes back live, the numbers stay, and one cluster at a time takes a doubled amber ring while a small card in the middle of the stage names it and says what it owns.

The card carries four controls and nothing else: pause, back, forward, close. Back and forward pause first — taking the wheel stops the clock, because a reader who reaches for “next” is reading at their own speed and a timer that keeps running would take the page away from them mid-sentence. Escape closes it, the arrow keys step it, and closing it puts the frame back exactly as it was found: no cluster left highlighted, no state left set, the circle-i dark again.

The tour is the one part that needs script

Three states are radios and work with scripting off; a timed walk cannot be. So the door ships hidden and the script removes the attribute — the button exists only where it would work. The tour also reads the clusters out of the frame itself rather than carrying its own copy of the list, so a cluster added to the rails is in the tour the moment it renders, and a caption that has drifted from the control it describes is not a failure mode this page has.

6Editor and viewer are the same framesaid, not impliedA frame that can be changed and one that can only be looked at wear the same rails. The difference is stated in the corner.

The temptation is to give an editable frame a second, richer set of controls and leave the read-only one bare. That is the wrong cut. The rails are the view's controls — where the eye stands and which layers are standing are questions a reader has just as much as an author — so they belong to both. What differs is whether the subject can be picked and changed, and that is one bit.

So it is said: the top-left corner prints Viewing or Editing, and the frame takes an inset accent rule while it is editable. Press Editing on the stage above and both change. Nothing else does — which is the point.

Why not just hide the rails on a read-only frame

Because the reader then has no way to look at the thing they were given. A read-only document view still needs zoom; a read-only model still needs to be turned around. Hiding the controls to signal read-only takes the view away in order to say something about the subject.

7The layer rail, and what it must not donamed, not numberedOne control per layer, carrying the layer's name and its colour. A hidden layer keeps its place in the stack.

Four controls, one per plate, each in the plate's own identity swatch so the rail and the subject agree without a legend. They are named, not numbered: a rail of four numbered checkboxes says nothing about what turning one off would remove, and the reader finds out by removing it.

Table 8The four plates of the stage's subjectinvented subject · four passes
PlateSwatchContributes
Groundp1all nine squares — the field
Formp47 squares
Markp75 squares
Glossp10one square — the centre
A hidden plate keeps its place in the stack. Closing the gap over it would move every plate above it, and the reader who turned one off to see what was underneath would watch the thing they were trying to look at slide out from under the pointer.

8What is underneath all of itno scriptThe same subject as flat isometric SVG, in the markup from the start, hidden only once a frame has actually been produced.

The fallback is not a placeholder graphic. It is the same four plates over the same ground, drawn flat, present in the markup before the module is fetched, and hidden only once the renderer has produced a real frame. The order matters: hide-then-draw leaves a blank rectangle for however long the module takes, and forever if it throws.

viewer.ts
renderer.setAnimationLoop(() => {
  ...
  if (!shown) { shown = true; host.classList.add("on"); }  // reveal after a real frame
});

Fig. 3 The same frame, caption and scope apply to a canvas as to a chart.

9Colour comes from the stylesheet0 hex hereMaterials read their tint out of the computed custom properties, so the stage follows the theme without a second palette declared for it.

Nothing in the module holds a hex. Each material reads a --pastel-* and a --stroke-* out of the computed style of the document element, so a theme change repaints the scene through a MutationObserver rather than through a duplicated palette that would drift on the first edit.

The temptation is to copy the six hexes into the module “just for the 3D”. That is exactly the fork that design-lint.ts exists to catch, and the linter reads the module too.

10What is in hand, and where it goesunder, not overThe decision in hand, stated as a decision, with the tool that decision actually takes -- on the edge the frame shares with it.

Rails act on the view. This acts on part of the subject, and that is a different job with a different rule: it has to be readable at the same time as the thing it changes. Press Editing on the stage and a strip appears joined to the frame’s bottom edge.

It floated over the lower left first, and that was wrong in a way worth writing down, because the argument for it was sound. A side inspector is worse: a viewport wide enough to be worth having is wide enough that a panel beside it is two glances away, so the reader carries the value across the page in their head. The mistake was concluding from that that it had to go on the frame. It only had to be near it. Over the frame costs the subject — the part being edited was under the thing editing it — and the cost compounded: a panel in the way needs a shut control, and a shut panel needs a badge to reopen from, so two controls existed only to walk back one placement decision. Joined to the bottom edge it is one glance, hides nothing, and needs neither.

Near the subject, not on it

When a control has to be read beside the thing it changes, the shared edge is what buys that, not the overlap. Reach for over-the-content only when the control is genuinely about a point in the content — a marker, a selection handle — and not when it is about a property of the whole.

The strip takes the frame’s own accent while the frame is editable, on the border the two share, so the pair reads as one object in one state rather than as a frame with a note under it.

a panel is not a rail

Table 9Three rules a panel keeps that a rail does not have tothe contract · every panel on a frame
RuleBecause
The head states the decision, not the encodingAn imperative with a subject — “choose the tint for the Form plate” — so a reader arriving cold knows what is being asked of them. plate 2, tone p4 is what gets stored, which is a different sentence and not one anybody asked for.
The tool wears the value’s own faceA colour is chosen from colours; a shape from shapes. A text field or a number is the right control only where the value genuinely has no other face, and reaching for one before that is how an editor ends up being a form about a picture.
It is up exactly while the frame can be editedOne bit, one owner, no second state to keep. The shut-state machinery went with the floating placement: a strip that is out of the way does not need to be dismissed, and a control that cannot be dismissed cannot be lost.

The swatches are the second rule made literal: the button is the colour, at the size of a word, carrying no text at all. The chosen one is ringed rather than filled darker — filling it would change the one property the reader is judging it by.

tokens-extra.ts
.vw-hand .hb-c{display:flex;gap:5px;flex:none}
.dk-tone{padding:2px;border:1px solid var(--rule);border-radius:3px}
.dk-tone[aria-pressed="true"]{box-shadow:0 0 0 2px var(--stroke-amber);
  border-color:var(--stroke-amber)}
Shut and empty are not the same state

Leaving edit mode does not clear the plate in hand. The two are independent, so coming back lands the reader where they left rather than at the start — the same argument as the reset that must not put the layer rail back.

The panel is also where the read-only case is settled. A frame that cannot be edited keeps every rail — looking is something a reader does too — and loses only the tool that writes. That is why the panel is bound to editing and nothing else is.

A control should say what it is about to do, not what is currently true. The label on a toggle reads “Stop the plates breathing”, not “animation: on” — plain English, verb first, and it changes with the state.

12A value with no word in it40 characters, 10 per rowAn address is not text. It is forty symbols a reader compares, and the default rendering makes comparing the reader's job.

Printed as a run of monospace it answers one question — here are forty characters — and leaves the only question anyone actually asks unanswered: is this the same account as the one I have. Nobody reads the middle. They read the first four and the last four, which is why every wallet in the world truncates to exactly that, and why the truncation is the honest default rather than a space-saving hack.

0xa1b2c3d4e5f60718293a4b5c6d7e8f90abcdef01
40 on one line20 per row10 per row8 per row5 per rowCopying takes the whole address; the cells are for comparing, not for editing. Nothing on this board writes. The magnifiers on the right border step the board between one line and five cells to a row.

The board makes that comparison a surface. Plain is the character. Ends dims the thirty-two nobody reads and leaves the eight they do. Value gives each cell a bar the height of its nibble, which turns the address into a small skyline — a shape two people can agree about over a video call in a way they cannot agree about c3d4e5f6.

Sixteen symbols have no colour vocabulary

The obvious move is a hue per hex digit. It is wrong here twice over: this site has twelve identities, all of them spoken for, and a reader does not convert a colour back into a digit anyway. A quantity gets a length. Colour stays reserved for the things a colour names.

The row length is a constant, not a minmax(). A board that reflows puts a different character under the same finger at a different window width, which is precisely the mistake the board exists to prevent; at a narrow width it scrolls instead. Same reasoning as the fixed row in the tile dock, where a folding address pushed the tool it belonged to off the bottom of the card.

tokens-extra.ts
.ab-grid{display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(var(--per),minmax(0,1fr));
  gap:3px;min-width:340px}
.ab-ends:checked ~ .ab-grid .ab-c{color:var(--ink-faint);background:transparent}
.ab-val:checked ~ .ab-grid .ab-c .vb{display:block}
Nothing on the board writes. A surface built out of forty buttons looks like an editor, so it has to say plainly that it is not one — the foot does, and the cells only ever select.

13Fields wear the site's faceno native selectA field is a name, a control and a note. The platform's chrome is what gets replaced -- never the input, which still carries the value and the keyboard.

A tool panel is mostly fields, and a default form control is the one element on a page that refuses the type, the spacing and the palette everything else agreed on. A native <select> opens an operating-system list in an operating-system font at an operating-system size, sitting inside a card built to 9.5px mono. That is not a taste objection. It breaks the one promise the rest of the frame makes: things that behave alike look alike.

Plate 3 · what this field panel writes
NameShown on the plate and nowhere else.
OwnerRead only in this build.
IdentityOne colour, one meaning.
Shape
Apart0stepsSame value the spread dock writes.
Breathing
Nothing is written until the panel is shut. The foot says what is stored, in the same words the fields used.

So the value keeps its element and loses its box. A text field is an <input> with a single bottom rule. A dropdown is a checkbox, two labels and a list of radios — it opens, it dismisses on the scrim, it records the choice, and it does all three with scripting switched off; the script only mirrors the chosen word onto the face. A number gets two hands instead of a spinner, and a switch is labelled with the sentence it is about to carry out, not the state it is in.

Wrong
<select><option>Peach</option></select>
<input type="number" min="0" max="9">
Right
<span class="fp"><input type="checkbox" id="fp1">
  <label class="fp-f" for="fp1">...</label>
  <label class="scrim" for="fp1"></label>
  <span class="fp-p"><label class="fp-o"><input type="radio" ...
Replace the chrome, keep the element

A div with a click handler is not a control. Everything above is still a label, a button, an input or a radio, so focus order, the keyboard, form submission and a screen reader all keep working. The moment a picker stops being radios it stops being reachable, and the only person who notices is the one who cannot use it.

The panel's foot restates what is stored, in the same words the fields used — the same rule as the tile dock, where a decision is stated as an imperative with a subject rather than as a setting name. A reader who has changed four things needs one sentence telling them what they changed, not four labels to re-read.

11What it costs2 draws/squareOne box geometry and one edge geometry for all thirty-six squares, and layout arithmetic that never touches a buffer.

Two draw calls per square — a solid and its edges — over two shared buffers, so the count does not grow with the instances. More important than the count: moving a plate does not rebuild it. Apart, fill and layer visibility all change positions and scales on groups that already exist; only a tone change or a wireframe toggle touches a material. Rebuilding meshes in order to move them is the single most common way a viewport like this drops frames on a phone.

The frame time and the draw-call count are printed live in the bottom-right readout. If the number stops changing, the loop is not running.

Back to the spec: index.html.
